summary.text: Writing the coefficient as a sum over triples satisfying \(N=n(k+1)+(n+1)j\), the proof pairs summands via \((n,k,j)\mapsto(j+k,k,n-k)\), with a binomial identity showing that paired weights agree. A fixed point has \(n=j+k\); if \(k<n\) its weight contains the even central binomial coefficient \(\binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}\), while the only remaining possibility is \(k=n\), \(j=0\), which forces \(N=n(n+1)\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(x)=\sum_{n\ge 0}x^n\frac{(1+x^n)^n}{(1-x^{n+1})^{n+1}}
      =\sum_{N\ge 0}a(N)x^N.
\]
We prove that if \(a(N)\) is odd, then \(N=k(k+1)\) for some nonnegative integer \(k\).

First expand each of the two factors in the summand indexed by \(n\). The binomial theorem gives
\[
(1+x^n)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk x^{nk},
\]
and the negative-binomial expansion gives
\[
\frac1{(1-x^{n+1})^{n+1}}
 =\sum_{j\ge 0}\binom{n+j}{j}x^{(n+1)j}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
x^n\frac{(1+x^n)^n}{(1-x^{n+1})^{n+1}}
 =\sum_{k=0}^n\sum_{j\ge0}
   \binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}
   x^{\,n(k+1)+(n+1)j}.
\]
For a fixed \(N\), only \(n\le N\) can contribute. Thus
\[
a(N)=\sum_{(n,k,j)\in T_N}W(n,k,j),                                      \tag{1}
\]
where
\[
T_N=\left\{(n,k,j)\in\mathbb N^3:
             k\le n,\quad N=n(k+1)+(n+1)j\right\}
\]
and
\[
W(n,k,j)=\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}.
\]
This is a finite set: the defining equation implies \(n\le N\), and then \(0\le k\le n\), while \(j\) is also bounded (and, for fixed \(n,k\), uniquely determined if it exists).

We now define a map on \(T_N\) by
\[
\Phi(n,k,j)=(j+k,\ k,\ n-k).                                                \tag{2}
\]
This map is well-defined. Indeed, because \(k\le n\), the third new coordinate \(n-k\) is nonnegative, and the new middle coordinate satisfies \(k\le j+k\). Moreover,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &(j+k)(k+1)+(j+k+1)(n-k)\\
 &\qquad=(j+k)(k+1)+(j+k+1)n-(j+k+1)k\\
 &\qquad=n(k+1)+(n+1)j=N.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the image again belongs to \(T_N\).

The map \(\Phi\) is an involution. If
\[
(n',k',j')=(j+k,k,n-k),
\]
then applying the same construction again gives
\[
(j'+k',k',n'-k')=((n-k)+k,k,(j+k)-k)=(n,k,j).
\]

The involution also preserves the weight. The weight at the image is
\[
W(\Phi(n,k,j))
 =\binom{j+k}{k}\binom{(j+k)+(n-k)}{n-k}
 =\binom{j+k}{k}\binom{n+j}{n-k}.
\]
Both this and the original weight are the same multinomial coefficient. Explicitly,
\[
\binom nk\binom{n+j}{j}
 =\frac{(n+j)!}{k!(n-k)!j!},
\]
while
\[
\binom{j+k}{k}\binom{n+j}{n-k}
 =\frac{(n+j)!}{k!j!(n-k)!}.
\]
Hence
\[
W(\Phi(n,k,j))=W(n,k,j).                                                     \tag{3}
\]

It remains to analyze the fixed points of this involution. A triple is fixed precisely when
\[
j+k=n,
\]
or equivalently
\[
j=n-k.                                                                      \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, under this condition all three coordinates in (2) remain unchanged, and conversely equality of the first coordinates of a triple and its image gives (4).

Write
\[
r=n-k=j
\]
at a fixed point. There are two cases.

First suppose \(r=0\). Then \(k=n\) and \(j=0\). The defining equation for \(T_N\) becomes
\[
N=n(n+1)+(n+1)\cdot0=n(n+1).                                                 \tag{5}
\]
Thus a fixed point of this type can occur only when \(N\) has the required form.

Now suppose \(r>0\), so that \(k<n\). The weight of the fixed point is
\[
W(n,k,r)=\binom nk\binom{n+r}{r}.
\]
Since \(n=k+r\), the following binomial-product identity holds:
\[
\binom nk\binom{n+r}{r}
 =\binom{n+r}{k}\binom{2r}{r}.                                               \tag{6}
\]
For example, both sides equal
\[
\frac{(n+r)!}{k!\,r!\,r!}.
\]
The central binomial coefficient in (6) is even whenever \(r>0\), because
\[
\binom{2r}{r}=2\binom{2r-1}{r-1}.                                            \tag{7}
\]
It follows that every fixed point with \(k<n\) has even weight.

We can now finish the parity argument. Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(a(N)\) is odd but that there is no nonnegative integer \(q\) with
\[
N=q(q+1).
\]
Partition the finite set \(T_N\) into its orbits under \(\Phi\). Every non-fixed orbit consists of two distinct triples, and by (3) their weights are equal. Its total contribution to (1) is therefore
\[
W+W=2W,
\]
which is even.

For a fixed orbit, the case \(r=0\) is impossible under the assumption on \(N\), by (5). Every remaining fixed orbit has \(r>0\), and its single weight is even by (6) and (7). Thus every orbit contributes an even integer to the sum (1). Hence \(a(N)\) itself is even, contradicting the hypothesis that it is odd.

Therefore there must exist some \(k\ge0\) such that
\[
N=k(k+1),
\]
as claimed.
